body.objective: Students will be able to name professions.
successCriteria: I can name professions in French
I can use masculine and feminine forms of job titles
I can describe what people in different jobs do
body.hook: Doctor, engineer, chef, programmer, nurse: in French, job titles often change for men and women. Knowing professions helps you talk about your future and understand job ads in bilingual Canada.

study.title: Les métiers
study.question: What jobs can I name and describe in French?
study.passage:
Job titles (written for this lesson):
Patterns: -ier → -ière (infirmier, infirmière); -eur → -euse (vendeur, vendeuse); -teur → -trice (acteur, actrice; agriculteur, agricultrice); -ien → -ienne (électricien, électricienne); same form with un/une (un/une journaliste, un/une architecte, un/une pilote). In Canadian French, many titles add -e: un ingénieur, une ingénieure; un médecin, une médecin.
Note: no article after être with professions: Elle est infirmière. (not "une infirmière")
Descriptions: Un infirmier soigne les patients à l'hôpital. Une programmeuse crée des applications. Un enseignant travaille dans une école. Une agricultrice cultive le blé en Alberta.
Activity: "Qui suis-je ?": students describe a job in three clues (Je travaille dans un hôpital. Je porte un uniforme. J'aide les malades.) and the class guesses.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
discussion: Which job titles have the same form for men and women?
What jobs are common in Alberta?
study.product: Describe five professions in French with masculine and feminine forms, where they work and what they do.

body.objective: Students will be able to talk about the future with futur proche.
body.iCan: I can talk about the future with futur proche.
successCriteria: I can describe future plans using the futur proche
I can explain my goals with reasons
I can ask others about their future plans
body.hook: "Dans dix ans, je vais être ingénieure. Je vais travailler à Calgary." Talking about your future combines everything: the futur proche, professions, places and reasons.

study.title: Mon avenir
study.question: What are my plans for the future?
study.passage:
Text (read aloud, written for this lesson):
Dans dix ans, je vais avoir vingt-quatre ans. Je vais étudier à l'université. Je voudrais devenir infirmière parce que j'aime aider les gens. Je vais habiter à Edmonton, mais je vais aussi voyager en France et au Sénégal. Mon but, c'est d'avoir un emploi intéressant et de parler trois langues !
Structures: Je vais + infinitive (I'm going to): Je vais étudier. Je vais devenir… Je voudrais + infinitive (I would like to): Je voudrais être pilote. Mon but, c'est de + infinitive: Mon but, c'est d'aider les autres.
Questions: Qu'est-ce que tu vas faire après l'école secondaire ? Qu'est-ce que tu voudrais devenir ? Pourquoi ? Où vas-tu habiter ?
Activity: partners interview each other with the questions, then write a "Dans dix ans" paragraph about their partner, using il/elle va.
study.source: Original text written for this lesson.
steps: Practise je vais, je voudrais and mon but c'est de
discussion: What does the writer want to become, and why?
What is the difference between je vais and je voudrais?
How might French help in your future?
study.product: Write a "Dans dix ans" paragraph about yourself with at least six futur proche sentences, one je voudrais and one reason.

body.objective: Students will be able to explain why French is useful.
body.iCan: I can explain why French is useful.
successCriteria: I can explain why French is useful in careers and life
I can name jobs that use French
I can present a persuasive argument for learning French
body.hook: Canada is officially bilingual, and many jobs, from federal government and diplomacy to tourism, health care and aviation, value people who speak French and English. Your French could open doors.

study.title: Pourquoi le français ?
study.question: Why is learning French useful for my future?
study.passage:
Reasons (written for this lesson from public sources):
Canada's two official languages are English and French, and many federal government jobs require or prefer bilingualism.
Jobs that use French: fonctionnaire fédéral (federal public servant), enseignant(e) de français ou d'immersion, interprète, traducteur/traductrice, infirmier/infirmière in bilingual hospitals, agent(e) de bord (flight attendant) with Canadian airlines that serve both languages, guide touristique, diplomate, journaliste at Radio-Canada.
Beyond jobs: travel to more than 50 countries where French is used, study in Quebec, France or Belgium, enjoy francophone music, films and books, and connect with francophone communities in Alberta.
Learning: research suggests learning a second language strengthens skills such as problem-solving and attention.
Speech structure (1–2 minutes): introduction with a hook; three reasons with examples; conclusion with a call to action ("Continuez à apprendre le français !"). Use: D'abord, … Ensuite, … Enfin, …
Activity: write and deliver the speech; the class votes on the most persuasive.
study.source: Summary written for this lesson; job examples are general.
discussion: Which reason is most convincing to you?
How did d'abord, ensuite, enfin help your speech?
Whose speech was most persuasive, and why?
study.product: Deliver a 1–2 minute persuasive speech in French giving three reasons to learn French, with examples and a call to action.
